p: Put a strip of zinc into copper(II) sulfate solution and the zinc becomes coated with copper: zinc atoms hand electrons **directly** to Cu²⁺ ions.
A galvanic cell does the same reaction with the two halves **apart**, so the electrons must travel through a wire, where they can light a bulb or turn a motor.
**Galvanic cell:** an electrochemical cell that converts the chemical energy of spontaneous redox reactions into electrical energy.

rules: **Anode (negative):** zinc, Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation). Zn is the stronger reducing agent (higher up on the right of Table 4).
**Cathode (positive):** copper, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction). Cu²⁺ is the stronger oxidising agent (lower down on the left).
**Electron flow:** through the external circuit, from Zn to Cu, never through the solution.
**Ion movement:** cations towards the cathode; anions towards the anode.

screens.q: In the zinc–copper cell, how do the electrons get from the zinc to the copper?
choices: Through the wire (the external circuit), from Zn to Cu.
Electrons flow only through the external circuit: the wire and the electrodes.
Through the salt bridge, from the zinc half-cell to the copper half-cell.
Electrons flow only through the **external circuit**. **Ions** carry the charge through the solutions and the salt bridge.
Through the wire, from Cu to Zn.
Electrons flow from the anode to the cathode. Zinc is oxidised: it is the anode.
screens.why: Electrons flow only through the **external circuit** (the wire and the electrodes). **Ions** carry the charge through the solutions and the salt bridge.

screens.q: A galvanic cell is made from a zinc electrode in 1 mol·dm⁻³ Zn(NO₃)₂(aq) and a copper electrode in 1 mol·dm⁻³ Cu(NO₃)₂(aq). (a) Identify the anode. Give a reason. (b) Write the half-reactions at the anode and at the cathode. (c) Write the overall cell reaction. (d) State the direction of electron flow in the external circuit. (e) State ONE observation at each electrode.

why: A learner writes the cathode half-reaction as Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu. How many marks does this lose, and why?
One mark ✓: SAGS requires a single arrow → in half-reactions and redox equations, and the memos deduct 1 mark for ⇌ (2023 memo, Q6.4: “Double arrow –1”); ⇌ is used only in Table 4 ✓.

p: Some half-reactions have **no solid conductor** to make an electrode from: Cℓ₂(g) + 2e⁻ → 2Cℓ⁻ involves a gas and an ion; Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺ involves two ions in solution.
**Suitable inert electrodes:** platinum (Pt) or graphite (carbon, C).
**Reasons:** it **conducts** electricity, and it is **unreactive**, so it does not take part in the reaction (it is not oxidised or reduced).

p: Cell notation describes a whole galvanic cell in one line. The anode half-cell is written on the left and the cathode half-cell on the right.
The order is always: reducing agent | product of oxidation || oxidising agent | product of reduction.

rules: Electrodes, including inert electrodes, are written on the **outside**: Pt | Cℓ⁻ | Cℓ₂ || F₂ | F⁻ | Pt
A single line | is a **phase boundary**: two species in different phases, in contact.
Two lines || are the **salt bridge**. Its electrolyte need not be shown.
Two species in the **same phase** are separated by a **comma**: Pt | Sn²⁺, Sn⁴⁺ || Fe³⁺, Fe²⁺ | Pt

screens.q: Which is the correct cell notation for the cell in which Mg + 2Ag⁺ → Mg²⁺ + 2Ag?
choices: Mg | Mg²⁺ || Ag⁺ | Ag
Anode half-cell on the left (Mg | Mg²⁺), cathode on the right (Ag⁺ | Ag), no coefficients.
Ag | Ag⁺ || Mg²⁺ | Mg
The anode must be on the left.
Mg | Mg²⁺ || 2Ag⁺ | 2Ag
No coefficients in cell notation.
Mg²⁺ | Mg || Ag | Ag⁺
The electrodes go on the outside.
screens.why: Mg | Mg²⁺ || Ag⁺ | Ag. Cell notation has **no coefficients**, even when the balanced equation needs them.

p: The further apart two half-reactions are in Table 4, the bigger the voltage of the cell made from them.
**E^{θ}_{cell} = E^{θ}_{cathode} − E^{θ}_{anode}**. Use both values **exactly as printed** in Table 4, with their signs. Never reverse the sign and never multiply E^{θ} by a coefficient.
For the zinc–copper cell: E^{θ}_{cell} = 0,34 − (−0,76) = **1,10 V**.

screens.h: Worked example 28.7: the emf of a cell
screens.q: Calculate the emf of a standard cell made from a Mg | Mg²⁺ half-cell and a Ag⁺ | Ag half-cell.

traps: E^{θ} does not depend on the number of electrons transferred, so it is never multiplied by a coefficient.
Put brackets round a negative E^{θ} before you subtract it: 0,80 − (−2,37).
Put brackets round a negative E^{θ} before you subtract it: 0,80 − (−2,37).
E^{θ}_{cathode} − E^{θ}_{anode}: silver is the cathode (+0,80 V), magnesium the anode (−2,37 V).

why: A learner writes 2(0,80) − (−2,37) = 3,97 V because the silver half-reaction was multiplied by 2. Explain the mistake.
E^{θ} does not depend on the number of electrons transferred ✓, so it is never multiplied by a coefficient: the emf is 3,17 V ✓.

screens.q: Use E^{θ}_{cell} to predict whether (a) copper reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid and (b) copper reacts with silver nitrate solution, under standard conditions.

ask.prompt: Work out E^{θ}_{cell} for H⁺ (the OA) and Cu (the RA).

traps: E^{θ}_{OA} − E^{θ}_{RA} = 0,00 − 0,34. Keep the sign: it tells you the answer.

ask.prompt: E^{θ}_{cell} = −0,34 V. Does copper react with dilute HCℓ?
choices: No: negative means non-spontaneous.
A negative value of the standard emf is an indication that a redox reaction is non-spontaneous under standard conditions.
Yes: any emf means a reaction.
The **sign** decides. Positive: spontaneous. Negative: non-spontaneous.
